taxonomic_note: Current Kew/POWO accepts Anatherum virginicum and treats Andropogon virginicus as a homotypic synonym. Retain the familiar Andropogon name as a primary search alias because most Texas field material still uses it.
look_here_first: Look for narrow silky racemes tucked partly inside flattened spathe-like upper sheaths. Mature plants often turn straw to orange-brown and hold the pale silky seedheads into winter. It does not make the dense brushy crown of bushy bluestem or the digitate turkey foot of big bluestem.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew accepts Anatherum virginicum and explicitly maps Andropogon virginicus into the accepted concept. USDA-derived county distribution under the familiar Andropogon virginicus name supports Hays, Real, and San Saba, all inside the project target zone.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Synonym-based county evidence is counted only because current Kew treatment explicitly links Andropogon virginicus to accepted Anatherum virginicum; do not infer counties from statewide or ecoregional presence.

best_field_traits: narrow silky racemes partly enclosed by spathe-like upper sheaths
silky hairs around spikelets create a pale fluffy look

seedhead branches remain narrower and less brushlike than bushy bluestem
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Anatherum glomeratum has a much denser, broader brushlike crown. Andropogon gerardi has open digitate turkey-foot racemes and a taller prairie-grass architecture.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Broomsedge has narrow silky racemes tucked in upper sheaths; bushy bluestem forms a dense brushlike crown, while big bluestem carries a few open turkey-foot racemes.

field_id_lesson.look_here_first: Broomsedge: follow a flowering culm upward and find many narrow silky racemes partly tucked into flattened leafy spathes, usually separated along the upper stem rather than packed into one bushy terminal crown. Brown winter color supports recognition but does not prove identity.
crew_checkpoints: Photograph the entire rooted clump and upper flowering stem, showing the spacing of spathe-enclosed units.
Open one mature spathe without destroying its connection to the stem; photograph paired racemes and the spathe with a millimeter scale.
Use a hand lens to document paired sessile and pedicellate spikelets, rachis hairs and awn attachment; record actual dimensions from the specimen.
Photograph the ligule and collar in focus, and compare the same structures against bushy bluestem.

look_alikes.check: Bushy bluestem produces a broad densely crowded brushlike terminal cluster of many short hairy racemes, unlike the more individually separated broomsedge spathes.
Little bluestem has silky racemes on distinct branches; compare branch arrangement, spathes and mature spikelet pairs rather than winter color.
Big bluestem usually shows a few exposed turkey-foot branches instead of numerous spathe-enclosed narrow units.

vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.source: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 Phytoneuron 2015-4 page 34, Texas Hill Country vegetative key
vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.look_here_first: Broomsedge can also have visible collar or sheath-edge hairs, despite a Texas Hill Country description of usually entire sheath margins. Do not exclude broomsedge just because you see hairs. Photograph the correctly identified inner AND outer margins and also compare the separate spathe-held flowering branches with bushy bluestem's crowded brush.
vegetative_bushy_vs_broomsedge.photo_handoff: Leaf/sheath micro PHOTO gap: need matched correctly determined living Texas specimens, one photo to prove inner opened SHEATH margin and a second to prove outer SHEATH margin, then the true collar/ligule and ruler. Existing USGS broomsedge leaf/stem photos show some hairs near the sheath, but neither is yet proven to show both identifiable margins with enough resolution. University/extension photos with unclear public reuse rights must not be installed.

field_caution.summary: IMPORTANT REVISION (2026-10-22): Do NOT key bushy versus broomsedge as simple 'hairy sheaths = glomeratum, hairless = virginicum'. The 2015 Texas Hill Country key describes hair on the distinct/open bushy sheath margins and generally entire broomsedge margins, sometimes with cilia on the outer edge. However Missouri, Texas A&M and Oklahoma sources explicitly show or describe broomsedge sheath or leaf-base hairs too. Species, growth stage, which margin is imaged, and geographic treatment can change the apparent difference. Inspect actual UPPER sheath shape and both separated margins on the SAME confirmed plant; treat hairs as one supporting character only. Big mature flowering architecture and measured rames/spikelets remain needed for confident separation.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.look_here_first: BROOMSEDGE: trace one culm upward to numerous SEPARATE narrow, silky flowering units, each with usually 2–5 short rames partly enclosed by an upper leafy spathe. Do not use orange-brown winter color or sheath hairs alone.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.growth_form: Warm-season, tufted perennial without spreading rhizomes; stems roughly 50–110 cm in Iowa/USFS treatments, flattened/keeled basal sheaths; blades often 2–5 mm wide. Rooted crown and flowering culm should be verified as one plant.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.ligule_collar: True ciliate membranous ligule is small, about 0.2–1.5 mm across regional treatments; leaf/sheath margin hairs are separate and variable, NOT a simple bushy-versus-broomsedge binary. Photograph unfolded inner and outer sheath margins plus true free ligule with 1-mm scale.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.flowering_architecture: Interrupted upper inflorescence; each spathe partly encloses commonly 2–5 slender hairy rames about 1–3 cm long. Hairy rachis internodes and companion pedicels must be distinguished from florets.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.spikelet_glumes: Each fertile sessile spikelet roughly 2.6–4.7 mm (Iowa 3.3–3.5 mm); pedicellate partner usually reduced/absent, leaving a silky-haired pedicel about 4.5–5 mm in Iowa. Two awnless glumes enclose the sessile spikelet; lower glume with two lateral keels, upper with one mid-keel; verify actual detached glumes before labeling.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.lemma_awn: Lower floret sterile with thin hyaline lemma; upper fertile floret has a deeply notched/two-lobed thin lemma bearing ONE slender awn from the sinus, often 6.5–18 mm in Iowa (broader treatments 6–26 mm). This is a LEMMA awn, not a glume awn; palea minute/absent in some descriptions.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261022.local_lookalikes: Anatherum glomeratum (bushy) crowds many short silky racemes into a broad brushlike terminal crown; A. virginicum has more separated spathe-held units. A. tenuispatheum is a distinct accepted species, not an A. glomeratum photo variant; compare its narrow raceme sheaths and measured spikelets with voucher. Schizachyrium scoparium has different upper-branch/raceme architecture; Andropogon gerardi has exposed turkey-foot fingers.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · START AT THE SPATHE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Several narrow silky racemes are partly tucked into leafy sheaths
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow one attached upper culm, not its winter color. Broomsedge is a warm-season tufted perennial; its narrow flowering units are commonly 2–5 short rames per spathe, mostly 1–3 cm long. Panel 1 shows gross flowering hairs, but cannot prove the number or attachment of individual rames.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN ONE SPIKELET PAIR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fertile sessile spikelet + reduced/absent pedicellate partner
field_id_short_tiles.details: At 10–20× look for a fertile sessile spikelet about 2.5–4 mm and a silky-haired pedicel, usually bearing only a rudiment or no companion spikelet. Identify two enclosing glumes and the thin fertile lemma carrying a straight awn roughly 7–25 mm, depending on treatment. These exact organs are NOT demonstrated by the existing photos; do not arrow hairs as a pedicellate spikelet.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Tiny fringed membrane; variable sheath-edge hairs
field_id_short_tiles.details: Unfold the blade–sheath junction and photograph the true ciliate membranous ligule beside a 1-mm ruler (published ranges roughly 0.2–1.5 mm). Separate the ligule from hairs on the upper blade or sheath margin. The current gallery does not resolve this structure.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · CHECK LOCAL BLUESTEMS
field_id_short_tiles.details: Anatherum glomeratum forms a broad densely crowded brushlike crown; broomsedge has more separate, narrow spathe-held flowering units. Little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) lacks the same prominent enclosing spathes. Anatherum tenuispatheum requires voucher-based anatomy; do not merge it into bushy bluestem or identify from a fluffy silhouette alone.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FINISHING EVIDENCE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Rooted plant + measured spathe, ligule and fertile lemma
field_id_short_tiles.details: To reach public-ready, obtain same-specimen Texas-vouchered rooted growth and complete upper flowering culm (cm scale), opened spathe/rames, true ligule, and dissected paired spikelets, glumes and awned lemma (mm scale). Verify image-level public rights and exact arrows against source pixels, then complete live-site QA. Until then retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · TRACE THE ROOTED CROWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial tuft, often keeled sheaths; winter copper color is not proof
field_id_short_tiles.details: Follow a flowering culm down to the same rooted bunch. Broomsedge is a perennial bunchgrass rather than a long-rhizomed colony; published culms are roughly 50–110 cm, with commonly 2–5 mm blades. Basal sheaths may be flattened or keeled, but sheath-edge hairs vary and overlap with bushy bluestem. Use the whole plant plus attached spathe-held racemes and measured sessile spikelets, never fall color or one hairy node, to decide. Existing gallery photos show standing culms and leaves but do not prove exposed roots or a dissected collar.
